messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Psychiatrist
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 47

He is 62 now, a psychiatrist with a careful voice and the habit of pausing before he answers even simple questions. In the hospital, residents know him as steady, formal, and unusually attentive to signs of fear in other people. They do not know that when a patient describes being trapped, restrained, or humiliated, he sometimes feels his own body tighten under his white coat. He keeps his hands folded so no one can see the tremor.

He grows up in Latin America during a period when politics enter ordinary life without warning. In his late twenties, before medical school is finished, he is involved in student organizing and community health work. He tells himself he is doing something practical and moral: helping in poor neighborhoods, speaking openly, believing that educated people have obligations. At first the danger feels abstract, something that happens to others, mentioned in whispers and cut off when strangers approach. Then one evening he is taken.

He remembers the arrest not as a single scene but as fragments with hard edges: a car door, rough hands at the back of his neck, the smell of gasoline and sweat, his face pushed down so he cannot orient himself. In the place where they hold him, there is no stable sense of time. Light appears and disappears. He is questioned for hours, accused of things he has not done, forced to listen to the screams of other detainees and to wonder if they are staged for him or real. He is beaten, deprived of sleep, threatened with death. At points he believes he will disappear there and that no one will ever know what happened to him. What remains with him most powerfully is not only pain, though he remembers that clearly, but the deliberate destruction of his sense of self: being made to beg for water, being mocked when he trembles, being forced to anticipate the next violation with no way to stop it.

When he is eventually released, there is no explanation. It feels less like freedom than abandonment. He returns home thinner, exhausted, and ashamed of how quickly fear has reorganized him. He notices that he startles at footsteps in the hallway and cannot tolerate closed rooms. He lies down to sleep and is back there immediately, feeling the pressure on his chest, hearing keys scrape metal. On some nights he wakes shouting; on others he does not sleep at all, sitting in a chair until dawn because sleep feels like surrender. During the day he avoids certain streets, certain uniforms, certain political conversations. If someone stands behind him in line, his heart pounds so hard he feels faint. He tells almost no one the details. In his family, survival is discussed through euphemism, and he learns to give a shortened version that leaves out the worst moments.

He leaves the country later and resumes his medical training with a ferocious discipline that looks, from the outside, like ambition. In truth, psychiatry offers him two things he cannot find elsewhere: a language for the injuries he cannot name in himself, and a way to remain close to suffering while staying useful. He becomes known for his composure. He listens well to trauma survivors because he recognizes the peculiar isolation in their speech—the way memory can be too vivid and unbelievable at once. Still, the work costs him. During emergency evaluations, if security staff enter suddenly or a patient must be physically restrained, a cold wave moves through him. For a split second he is no longer an older physician in control of a room but a captive waiting for the next blow. He recovers quickly enough that colleagues rarely notice, but afterward he feels drained, irritable, and embarrassed by how immediate it is.

He has never married. He says this matter-of-factly, but over time it becomes clear that intimacy has always carried danger for him. In relationships he is attentive and generous until he feels expected to depend on someone; then he withdraws, stops returning calls, works later, claims fatigue. He does not like anyone seeing him asleep. Even now he checks locks more than once and chooses seating in restaurants with a view of the door. He dislikes being touched unexpectedly and masks this with a joke or a small sidestep. Loud banging noises, the smell of damp concrete, and men shouting in another room can ruin the rest of his day.

What troubles him most in the present is that the past does not stay past. He is successful, respected, and outwardly calm, yet he lives as if danger remains nearby. Nightmares still come in clusters. Some mornings he arrives at the hospital already tired from having fought his way out of sleep. He avoids news from his home country, then feels guilty for turning away. Certain patients stay with him too intensely; after hearing their stories, he finds himself sitting in his office long after clinic ends, staring at the wall, his body braced. He understands exactly what is happening in clinical terms, but that knowledge does not protect him from it. He says, with a sad half-smile, that he has spent his life helping other people name terror while continuing to organize his own around silence, routine, and the hope that vigilance might still keep him safe.
